blocks.x: That's right. Anything you want to ask, Mac, will be fine, too.
Now, first of all, let me ask you before you go ahead and cut anything.

I'll make a note on here that we're recording Mr. Don Albert at his home. It's 715 St. James in San Antonio for the Tulane University Archive of Jazz. And this is Bill Russell. And then Mac Fairhurst from Ohio is also here tonight. And we'll be talking about some of his records. Do you mind telling us when you were born and your birth date and where you were born?

Well, Bill, I'm always proud of that birthday. I was born August 5, 1908 in New Orleans, Louisiana. I was born at 1719 North Robertson Street. My daddy still lives there. He's living in the same home. And the funny part about it, he doesn't own the home yet.
You mentioned that I was to see your father about a month ago. And talked to him a few minutes, but we didn't get to interview him. He wasn't in a mood to be interviewed, he said, that day.
Yeah, well, that's the type of fellow he is.
Some days he won't talk to anybody. People call him grumpy. But he was very pleasant that day. And he did tell me how old he was then. 84 he is now, isn't he?
That's right.
He was born the same day as your uncle, Natty Dominic. Dominic. Oh, you might mention your name originally was Dominic.
My name is Dominic. I use it, but my professional name is Don Albert. The last part's always added for writing checks. It's still legally then your name. That's right. My name is Dominic.
Do you mind telling a little bit about your teachers or how you got started in music?

Well, it's a peculiar thing how I got started in music. My daddy was a violin player and he wanted me to learn the violin. And I just couldn't stand screeching on that E note. So I decided to become a singer. I was just a little kid and my daddy would take me all over these different clubs in New Orleans like the Autocrat Club. They usually got together bands with the members of the club and they had some real good bands. And they would have these little talent programs, as they called them. They weren't called those in those days like they are now. And I decided to go on out for singing and I did pretty good as a country singer.
I know your Uncle Natty says that your father was a very fine singer.

My father was a great tenor voice. He sang with some of the great singers, Burt Williams and some of the other singers that were down there. They probably don't recognize his name now. But he sang where the old French opera house was down there. Only thing about my daddy, sometimes he was a little stage fright. But outside he had a great voice. Well, after I decided that I didn't have too much of a voice, I decided that I wanted to play trumpet.
How old were you when you started taking this up?

Well, the trumpet, I think I was around the ages of eight, nine or ten, somewhere in that area. And the man that I wanted to play like, it was a very peculiar thing. His name was Nelson Jean. They spell it J-E-N, Jean, but it's pronounced Jean. French. That's correct.
Did you learn French when you were a boy?
Well, I talk French. My grandmother and everyone talk French to us. We never did get anything talked to us but French.
I know Natty said he was raised that way.

On French, that's right. And I still talk French now. And then when someone, when I can talk with someone. So the first lesson I had at Nelson Jean's house, he was a great friend of the family, but he liked to take a drink of wine. So I went on my first lesson. And then, while he told me to get, had an old cornet that I bought somewhere. I don't know where it was. And anyhow, my daddy found it for me, I believe. And I was too young to remember. He wanted me to learn how to clean the horn. So I decided to clean the horn on the first lesson. And the lessons were on Sunday. So he told me to come back the next Sunday. I went back the next Sunday and I found Mr. Jean in the same condition that I found him in the first Sunday. And he told me to clean the horn again. So I came. I told my daddy. I said, well, I don't want to learn music. I said, all this fellow's doing is teaching me how to clean the horn. Well, I was just a little kid. And so I imagine I took an offense to it. Well, my cousin, Bonnie Big, who's now with Louis Armstrong, he and I came up together almost like brothers. And he was learning. And he was learning from one of the greatest clarinet players that I have ever heard of musically. And also as a player. And that was old man Lorenzo Teo. Originally from, he's from Mexico City.
We talked to one of the brothers of the old men. There was an old Lorenzo and a Louis Teo, Papa Teo.
Well, that's the old man. Papa. That's what we call him.
And there's now, there's still a Louis Teo living who was a brother of young Lorenzo, the very fine clarinetist.

So one brother is still living there. He's still living, but I don't remember him. But the one that finished, well, anyhow, Bonnie went to, he says, well, come on, Papa, I'll take you over. So I went over to one day with him. And Bonnie took his lessons first. Then after he went through his, he was already playing the clarinet, but I hadn't even decided on the horn yet. So, old Papa called me over there as we called him. He says, well, come on, let's get to learning these notes here. So he went to teaching me the fundamentals of music. All about the parts, the notes, and everything else concerned with music. Not about any particular instrument. So Bonnie had a peculiar way of doing something like this in his nose.
Oh, really?

And I thought he was laughing at me. So I didn't go back then anymore. So Bonnie saw me about a month late. He says, how come you haven't been back to lessons, old Papa, asking about you? Or I said, Bonnie, you sitting over there laughing at me. I said, I can't learn anything. He said, I wasn't laughing. He says, I do that on account of some sand in my nose that I got when I was swimming. Oh, I said, well, I'm not going back anyhow. So a thought struck me then that I better go on and learn some music somewhere because I wanted to learn. Most of my family were musicians. Then my father contacted my last teacher, Mr. Piran. And I studied my soft edge and my music for one year and a half singing the notes in time. Before you took up the carnet. Before I took up the instrument.
Natty had to do that with Manuel Perez.

That's right. A long time. A lot of the old time teachers were that way. Well, Manuel lived right opposite Uncle Natty's house on Erdworth Street. And I used to watch Manuel when he'd come in from work and when he'd leave. In the evenings, I used to follow the parades. I used to follow the bands. That's the one that Louie came out of. I used to love to hear those kids play those horns. I'd follow them for blocks.
That's a tuxedo or the honours band.

No, I'm talking about those two, but I'm referring to the boys from Jones's home. Oh, the Jones's home. That Louie had gone. And they all impressed me as very, kept wanting me to want to learn music. So after I studied my solfege and my music, I decided that a cornet is what I really wanted to play. And I went from there. I studied the...
You still had your old cornet that your father...

No, I let that one go. In fact, I don't have any of my old instruments. Some of them had been stolen. Some of them had been lost. And unfortunately, there are things that I... Even the books that I learned in were stolen from me.
That's too bad.
Do you remember the method that you studied? Clodermere.
I don't know.

The old French method. Clodermere. It's one that I'd want to keep. I even imprinted my name and asked if the founder ever found this book, please return it. But I imagine someone stole it. It wasn't lost. Someone stole it.
Funny world. People will take something that they can't possibly use.
Can't use it. Now, that's a book I'm sure that they couldn't use. It was written. Most of the words were in French.
Natty says he got one. And Manuel Perez sent to Paris. And God was all in French mostly, too.
Most of those books. And those are the books that I used. They were handed down.
They were what we call handed down books. Natty couldn't remember the name of the method, though. Who's the writer of it? No.
It's Clodermere. That's correct. You know how that's spelled? Those French names. C-L-O-U-D-I-M-I-E-R-E. Clodermere. I think that's correct.
While I think of it, I wonder if you could tell us a little bit more about your father, since we may not ever get to talk to him. He's 84 now, you say. That's correct. Or was on last August the 4th.
No, August the 2nd. August the 2nd. Your birthday. I'm on the 5th.
The 5th. Very near.
That's right.
Strange. Both your uncle and your father born the same day.
That's right.
You mentioned he studied violin. Who was this teacher? Did he ever talk to you much about it?

Yes, there were two or three men involved with him. One of them was the old man, Valtair, that I can remember vividly. And the others came from within the family. I had an uncle that was a great violin player. He died real young. Naval. They call him Naval.
Don't remember that name before.

No, he was real young when he died, but he was a great violin player. Then, too, there was another trumpet player in the band, another one of the young brothers. His name was Wilson. That's before Uncle Matty knew. But he died young. Unfortunately, the family was, in those days, passing young. So my daddy got an inspiration from those playing. And people in the family, Pierron was a violin player. Exchange their lessons with each other.
Your father, a month ago, mentioned something about this Mr. Augustine. Do you remember?
I can't know who he's talking about. He may be referring to George Augustine, that was the bass player.
I think he did mention he was a bass player, but I don't remember now if he played with him or studied something with him or what it was.
They probably played together.
Maybe played together.
Because, as I say, in these clubs like the Autocrat, mostly the members would get together on a Sunday afternoon and they would assemble there and they would play.
I remembered one time in the conversation your father mentioned George Moret, too.
Well, George Moret was one of the great trumpet players.
Yes. You know, if your father might have played with him or something?

Well, sure, we lived around the corner from that. That's how we happened to mention it. That's right. Well, George Moret happens to be, I find this, that over a period of years that these guys giving jazz histories have failed to mention George Moret. He was very conservative and a fellow that wouldn't go out the way to make himself seen or known. But far as playing the cornet, he was one of the best. He was during the time of Manuel, Manuel Perez.
I know Louis Armstrong mentioned him in a series of interviews.
Yes, I just want to say that, that Louis Armstrong is the only one that happened to mention in his biography of George Moret.
And last summer in New Orleans, they had a series of three TV interviews. And he talked again about hearing old man Moret. He always calls him in the parades. That's right. And how good he was.
That's right.
So Louis mentioned him a few times, several times. That's right. So your father lived right around, and you lived right around the corner from him.
We lived right around the corner from Mr. Moret. My grandfather lived right opposite Manuel Perez. In fact, Piro and all of them, T.O., were right in the Seventh Ward, as we call it.
You remember, were you still in New Orleans when Mr. Moret died? I don't know anything about him.

Yes, I was a little fellow. He's been dead then a long time. Oh, years and years. Yes, I used to go and stay at his house with his wife and his daughter. They used to consider me, as they called me, a play son.
Yes, we know nothing at all about him, his life, the facts of how old he was. Did he usually lead his own band?
Yes, he played mostly at the West End and Spanish Ford.
Yes.
And he played the parades.
Did he have his own brass band, too?

I don't remember whether he had his own brass band or not, but I do know that he played with the major brass bands over there. And I can remember vividly that Boccage and those musicians played with him at West End. And so did Bonnie Bigard when Bonnie was just learning.
Peter Boccage is still playing and going strong.
Played a parade about two weeks ago on Sunday.
He did? Yeah. Plays with the Eureka Band.
Fine.
Before we played last week ago, Thursday night. Week ago. What is tonight? Thursday? Yeah. One week ago tonight. Right.
That's right.
He was in my record shop. They played down at the Cabildo. They had a special program at the Cabildo with the Eureka Band, and he played with that program.
Well, where is your record place?
I have a little place on 731 St. Peter Street.
Oh, you're in the French quarters?
Right in the French quarters.
Oh. Oh.

And the band stopped up there after they needed to get their check cash, and they came up to see if somebody else could cash it across the street. Larry Bornstein didn't. And I happened to have the cash there. Yeah. Yeah. I cashed the check for them, and I got paid them that night. But Peter looks quite well. He's gray-haired and thinner than he used to be, but he plays very well. And he made some records about in February, Mardi Gras time, with his own little dance band, and it sounded very good.
I think some of the old regs. Well, I intend going back to New Orleans in July on a short visit, and I've contacted my personal friend over there, Paul Barbaran. Oh, yes.
We see him.
Yes, and I'm going to sit in with him when I get down there on a few of the jazz numbers. And I'm going to sit in with him.

I know that I'm going to resume some old friendships down there with some of the other guys, such as Professor Manuel Monnetto over in Al Jays and most of these other fellows that I know around there that knew me.

By the way, Fess, I see him almost every Tuesday night. A friend of mine studies clarinet with him, and I go over and record the lessons on tape just to get his ideas on music, and he talks a little bit about the old times. And he still has your card up on the wall.
He does.
It may be this same card. That's right. I'm not sure if it's the same one. It all started to turn brown.
Well, you see, Fess came here and spent a couple of weeks here with me.
And he said to be sure and give you his regards. I would have forgotten if you hadn't brought up his name and so many things to think of.
That's right.
And Fess has sort of retired, but he still has a few music pupils. He's taught many musicians. Oh, yes.
Many musicians. He has taught them.

Great man. I have over a hundred tapes about him. The complete story of his life. He's a great talker, a very slow talker. That's right. He has a wonderful memory and has played so many years. Started about 1907 or so playing professionally. And he gave up playing about 1922 or so. Did you ever study with him by any chance?
No, I never had to. I didn't study with him. You'd left. I had left New Orleans. The only real professor I had, like I said, was Mr. Piran.
Did he, on the trumpet itself, did you learn from Piran? Did he help you on the trumpet then?
No, I learned on the cornet.
On the cornet, I mean.

That's all. And when he found out he didn't want me to play in bands and jazz bands. He wanted me to be a Finnish musician first. When he found out that I was playing little gigs around there, he said, well, you know too much now. You better go on on your own. And so that's when I decided, well, I wouldn't stay in New Orleans. The field was better for me to complete my musical career outside of New Orleans.
What kind of a band did you have there or did you play with in your first jobs?

Well, I played with a fellow named Bill Phillips. He's a drummer. He's still around there. But I never will forget my first job. I played on Mardi Gras there on the truck. I could play three songs. The Sheik of Araby, I Love You, and some other rhythm song. I can't remember what that one was. But we got up in the Irish Channel and a fellow called me off on the side. He said, look here, fellow. He says, can't you play anything with those three songs?
He's been following you around, huh?

He was one of the masters. So I said, yeah, I can play something else. So I started out and I tried to improvise one of the three I was playing. He says, that's the same one you've been playing all the time. But in volume it all, huh? He says, that's the same one. Right on the truck then. Yeah, that's right. Well, I left Mardi Gras with three pieces. I left there with the banjo, Richard McCarthy, and Lucian Johnson. And my first stop was Dallas, Texas. And I played at a honky-tonk in Dallas, Texas. It was on the central track, central and west. Tip-top, I think they called it. And another great trumpet player was playing around there. He's dead now. Lee Collins.
Oh, yes. I knew him. Very much in Chicago.

That's right. Well, Lee was playing in the same neighborhood. And that's when Troy Floyd came to town. And I was a fellow who always liked to follow musicians. And I happened to go to a party I was having there for Troy. Troy was a great man then. And I got to talking to some of the guys in his band and also Trent's band. So Chester Clark, which is another great trumpet player, said, why don't you try to get that job with Troy's band? He says, Claude Kennedy's leaving. Oh, I says, I don't know if I could play good enough to play in that band. He says, sure you can. He says, you can read, can't you? I said, I'll read anything. Well, Troy just told me, well, come on, you'll go on the job with me. And the first job was in eastern Texas. And when I tuned my horn up, a guy touched me on the back. He says, gee whiz, man, how you get such a tone out of your horn? Well, I says, I don't know. I'm just playing like I learned. So by the tonation is the reason why I got the job with Troy. But I still could read the music at sight, which I still do. Even though not playing like I'm supposed to be playing, I still can read the music at sight.
After having that self-edged training for a year and a half, that comes to see for you.
I really did. That's right.
Can you tell us about those records when they were made and where and so on?
No, I know definitely that the records that I cut here.
Yes, this is from, we might mention that this is the article from the Olin Blackstone's playback magazine, February 1949. We have a copy of that.
That's right.
I haven't looked at it for a couple of years or longer.

Those numbers, True Blue Lou, Rockin' and Swingin' and The Sheik of Arabee, You Don't Love Me, Deep Blue Melody on the Sunny Side of the Street and Liza and Also Tomorrow. Those were arrangements by some of the men in my band with some of my ideas. And if I'm not mistaken, those records were cut somewhere in 1930 or 31, just before I left from New York City or possibly a little bit later. Now, I can't recall a date on these records.
That's close enough, at least we know within two or three years. That's right.
They were cut here at the old hotel. It's still in existence, the hotel, the Blue Bonnet Hotel. It was a makeshift room.
Right here in San Antonio.
In San Antonio. The other recordings I cut with the various artists were in Dallas, Texas.
We mentioned the Hattie. Hattie Burleson.
Burleson and Ben Norrisingle.
Ben Norrisingle, that's right. And you say you worked in his band then too or how was that? In whose band? Ben Norrisingle.
Did he have a band? No, he was part of Troy Foer's band, wasn't he?
No, he wasn't. He was just a singer. No, he wasn't in Troy's band.
This band that Ben Norrisingle sings these records, on these records with, were a group out of the Troy Foer's band. That is correct.
That's right. That part is right. Because one of them still lives here in San Antonio is the old man now, Charlie Dixon. He has all of those recordings.
Uh-huh.

Is there anything you can tell us about the vocalian records you made under your own name? Oh, by the way, another man I saw, I met on the street the day before I left, that was on Monday, is Louis Cottrell, the clarinetist. Sure. He's president of the union now. That's correct. And also an insurance collector or something. That's right. He was going down St. Peter's Street, and as I walked out of my door, and I was in a hurry, he said, I'm going over to Texas, and I hope to see one of your old friends over there. And I said, tell him hello for me.
Well, here's his name right here.
Yeah.
He was one of the, he was an original member in my band.
I said, how long were you with the band? He said, oh, nine years. He gave the date, something like up to 1938 or something. I forget. That's right.
This is Cottrell's, Cottrell's daddy was a great drummer.
Yes, we've, a lot of people have told us about him.
Oh, he was great. I used to love to see him come in in the morning with his drum strapped on his back. That's how they carried the drums.
Well, he did? I didn't notice. The bass drum? The bass drum on the back and snare drum in his hand. You know, some people tell us about one time he had a collapsible drum that folded up.
I don't know.
I don't remember that. Made out of something like aluminum, something like. I think I recall that. I never did see one myself.
I think I recall that. Not positive. I want to say for sure that I do. But offhand, I do remember him carrying a small package.

Anything, let's see, Alvin Alcorn, of course, was over here for a while, I understand, and played with you. He was interviewed for Tulane, too, but I've never heard his interview. Another fellow up there, Dick Allen, interviewed him.

Well, yes, he was a mainstay in my band for years. I got Mickey. We call him Mickey. Mickey Alcorn. I brought him out of New Orleans when he was a kid, too. I never heard him call that Mickey. Mickey. I never heard him. Just when you see him, say, hi, Mickey. Yeah. I never heard anybody call him that over there.
He still plays the parade. Oh, he's fine.
He's a good musician. He played with George Lewis the last time I heard him up in Columbus, Bill.
He made a trip to Europe with Kidori, too, about four years ago.
That's right.
How long was he with you?
He stayed with me all around eight or nine years.
That's long term.
I started him when he was a real young fellow. Real young fellow.
Anybody else from New Orleans over here that you can remember besides Cottrell?
Here in San Antonio?
Yes.

No. The last one that was here was my drummer, Fats Martin, and he passed away, oh, about three or four years ago. Well, in fact, he took the remnants of my band and kept going when I gave up. And I stayed with him until he passed, and everybody knew him as a great drummer.
Is there anything else about the recording date, wherever those records made, for Vocalion? Here in town? Here in San Antonio.
That's right.
And is the date given there? Is it accurate and all that you remember?
Yes, it says 35 or 36.
Anything else about the tunes? I don't remember all of them. I haven't heard those records for quite a while.
Well, I tell you what, I have a master on these records, and if you're interested in wanting to hear it or want a copy of it, I'd be happy to let you take it off.
Someday we might want to do that if we don't find the originals.

Well, I have an original of the Shadowland Blues, the one that was made with Troy Floyd, and I played a solo on the other side. And I have also a master record on one of these numbers. I think it's True Blue Lou. But the other is a copy from a jazz enthusiast that picked it up in Europe and gave it to Herbert Hall. It was my clarinetist and also my alto man.
Oh, it's Herbert Hall. Is that the brother of Edmund Hall? That's correct.
That's the one that's playing with Jimmy Condon.
Yes. In the New York night.
That's right.
Sounds somewhat like Edmund a little bit.
He does. Almost exactly. Is he younger than Edmund? Oh, yes. A whole lot younger. He's one of the younger brothers.
There's still a couple of them over there. Clarence Hall, I think, is a male man. That's right.
He still plays tenor.
Yes, plays tenor. Can you tell us anything about the engagements that your band played and your club, if you can bring that into the council, the Keyhole Club and all?
The engagements that we had over the United States?
Yes, different places. Did you travel much?

Well, we traveled every night for almost ten years. We covered 38 states. We covered most every city in every state. You take the state of Texas, which is the largest state in the United States. We covered four corners of Texas. It's not a city in the state that we even far west Texas, a little bit of towns like Pampa. We played those towns, Odessa, before they were ever brought up to in population like they are now. We didn't miss any towns. In Louisiana, we found backwards that we didn't even know existed in Louisiana. And played those towns. And in those days, the bands usually played mostly percentage dates. We got by playing percentage dates. Because the guarantees were very scarce, very, very scarce. In fact when we went to New York City, when Joe Glazer took me under his wing, the reason why I left him was because he was holding out for big guarantees from a band and we could live better by our percentage dates coming back south. That's the only reason why we left Glazer's office. Did you play in New York at all, Don? Yes, we played in New York. We played at the Follies Theater over there in Brooklyn with Ralph Cooper and his review. We were built at the Apollo. And we also played a few other spots. We went into the Renaissance on one date, on a dance date.
What year would this be then, Don?
We went to rehearsal from Buffalo, New York into New York City in about 1932, 1933.
Do you know whether Charlie Johnson was still playing around New York then or not?
Charlie Johnson, I can't recall the name. But I know that the Cotton Club was then on 147 in Lenox. Because we went down there for an audition when Duke was playing in there.
Did you play maybe Small's Paradise? Yeah, that's right.
Charlie Johnson, that's right. Small's Paradise on 135th, I think it is, 135th and 7th.
You never run into a horn player by the name of Jabbo Smith, did you? Oh, I knew Jabbo. You did?
Oh, yes, I did. Sure.
I know Jabbo quite well.

The guy that's playing now that's doing such a terrific job now that's just now got a good break. What's his name? Making all these fine records. Oh, my goodness. I can't call his name as well as I know him. Well, he worked with me in Buffalo, but he's on his own now. Is he Roy Eldridge? No, Roy. This is one of the old timers that's playing this good, good...
Oh, Jonah Jones? Jonah...
Jonah Jones. Well, sure, sure. Sure.
Well, he finally...

got a break. He's doing all right now. Jonah's playing the same trumpet now that he was playing then. Only then he was playing more than what he's playing now. Yeah, the same thing is true of Sidney DeParis. You probably know Sidney DeParis too and Wilbur DeParis. That's right. Sure. They're playing fine today. Finally getting a little recognition to him. That's right. Well, Jonah deserves it. He's a good man. Sure he does. Is there anything you'd like to add
about the Keyhole Club or when you organized that? Well, the Keyhole first came into being in 1944

and I closed it in 1948 and I thought I wanted to go to New Orleans and open a massive club down there and I sold out everything I had there and went to New Orleans and I found out that the ways of living down there was different from the ideas that I have in regards to nightclub and also to music and shows. The tradition down there seems to remain in the same vein. So in going down there I lost a lot of money in about three months' time and I wasn't trying to get any music down there for myself so I went into the post office and in 1950 I came here to San Antonio to open this present Keyhole that I have which has been a landmark here.
I know it's been here for years I heard.

1950 was the first Easter Saturday when this one was first opened and I have used all of the major performers and bands in the place and I have started a lot of them off on their careers and they've gone to the top. In fact one of the men, Henry, has been on all the major networks for the last six months now and I started out at the Keyhole. Well I intend to start playing some music again.
That would be wonderful. We'd like to hear you again. I know a lot of people would.

You certainly would. Well in fact I'm doing it mostly for some friends out of New Orleans that have dug up some of this jazz history on my background and I feel that if it's in my power to come back and do the things that I know how to do in music and if it'll make someone else happy along with making me happy which is the fundamental thing well I'm more than happy to do so. In fact I had my friend in New York City has often tried to get someone interested in this, Franklin Dregs.
I know he's been interested in for years in the music of the whole southwest as he calls it from Kansas City on down to Oklahoma and Texas. That's right. He's been quite a number of articles on that.

There's been a lot, a lot of fine blues singers that's come out of this Texas area and you can't and often times they're accompanied by maybe a tuba and a piano or a guitar and a piano and you can't tie the things in in any way. There's not enough knowing about them. That is correct. I agree to that. I think that there should be, if you could just find or run across one of the Nolan persons, that would be the only way you'd be able to ever be able to tie this stuff together.
Well if I heard, if I heard the records, if I heard the performer I could tell you.
Someday when we get back we can either bring a tape.
Well you have them all on tape, Bill, that Dick took there at the university. Next time you come back you can plan for a dollar.

If I had known I would have picked up that tape. Well like I said Bill, now I'm going to New Orleans in July and if you would want me to drop by there, well I'd be more than happy to come by and go through a little bit more with you because there's so many things down there that I could recall by being there that I can't recall here.

I'd be glad to show you some of the old pictures and things we've collected too. We've been collecting quite a few, some of the old sheet music, everything that we can find, the old records. And of course our main job are these interviews to get the facts right straight from the musicians.
Well like I said, I would be more than happy to give you the part that I know because I can go way back to even to the days when Buddy P.T. was playing down there.

Well I was going to ask a little bit more, we're just about out of this tape, it's a half hour and it's been going to take another five minutes if you don't mind, talk a little bit about some of the other trumpet players you heard when you were young and some of these brass bands. Let this run on through here for a second or we can keep on talking until it's over. You mentioned hearing Louis Armstrong in this little Jones' home band. Do you remember what kind of dates they played, regular parades?

Well I was a little too young to recall that. I was just a kid in my knee pants but I vividly recall running to the corner of my house when the parade would be coming. It would be just a band playing, ordinary street parade. And I just would stand up there and watch them. After I learned my horn and I got to playing music professionally, as I say professionally, I worked on the boat that crossed from Spanish Fork to Mandeville, the Susquehanna.
Oh yes, I've heard about that.

We would go on the boat at a certain time and start playing music. We'd play until the Susquehanna landed over in Mandeville. Then we would get off and go around the town until time for the boat to leave then. That's why I made a great friendship over there with one of the greatest trumpet players that I have ever heard, and that was Buddy Petit. Buddy lived in Covington and Mandeville, all those places are right close together, so I would frequent him quite a lot. Then like I said, Mr. How did he sound? How did Buddy describe any of it? The greatest. And there was Kid Punch. He's still around. Oh, he was a great finger man, as we call it. Then there was Chris Kelly. Oh yes. Chris Kelly had the most beautiful tone in the trumpet a man could ever want to hear. Really? Oh, he was marvelous.
People tell us he was wonderful on the blues like Careless Love, but was he good on other things too, everything? Or what style did he have?

Well, as far as I can remember, I just would sit up there and I used to go up there and listen to those bands play. They used to play in what we call the buzzard roof in these dance halls. We had to go upstairs. Oh yeah, the balcony. Upstairs in the balcony. And I used to go up there just a kid and sit down. I'd sit next to Buddy and just listen to him play. As far as I'm concerned, he played everything. Of course, Manuel Perez was at the Roof Garden. And there he had a great banjo player with him. I have never heard another man play as much. That was Caffrey Dyeronsburg. I very seldom hear these jazz musicians talk about him.
Yes, George Dano talks about him, says he was wonderful. And the younger banjo player over there, he started in 1927. He talks about...
Well, the reason why I believe they don't talk too much about Caffrey. Caffrey was a little touchy. He was awful touchy.
Is he any relation to Joe Dyeronsburg, the clarinet player? I asked...
I talked with Joe when I was in California. I doubt seriously whether there's a close connection there or not. He's a fine fellow.
He's a fine fellow. Oh yeah, I know Joe. I talked with him when I was in Washington. I did too.

There's another Dyeronsburg who played violin in New Orleans. Yes, that's another old one. But they don't tie in together with this Caffrey. Caffrey had a brother Percy, but both of them died in Dallas. But Caffrey Dyeronsburg, I often hear guys talk about great banjo players. There were only two. And Caffrey was one of them. And John Moreira was the other. Yeah.
Lawrence's brother. We knew Lawrence.
Yeah, we knew Lawrence and this was Bill John. Yeah, but now Lawrence is one of the guys that... That's my son. How are you?
Mac Ferrer, who's that? Bill Russell. This is Bill Russell. Please know him.
Talking about old time music with your father. Getting some of the history down. You were talking about the other banjo players.

Yeah, well you see I knew Lawrence. I played with Lawrence, but I always considered John as an artist. As everybody says that. And then naturally you had another brother, Simon, that was the bass player. And those guys could really play.
Yeah, their father was a famous old time bass too.

Yes, he was. I never heard of him. Same way as Bob Rand's daddy. He's an old time... He died last year. Yeah, I understand he did. In June. He had a big funeral. Yes, I understand he did. And so with Piku, I... Well, that was the biggest in history almost. Yes. Well, I played a few dates with Piku. I played with him in a little town in Louisiana. We called it the De La Cua Islands.
Oh yes, down there. Way down in the bottom.

Where Spanish people know that. That's right. Then I played with him on a couple of the trucks down there. And when I had gone back on a visit to New Orleans. And Piku and I were great friends. Because I had a cousin down there, Armand Pierron, which I have one of his numbers here that Crawford sent me in one of his arrangements. This happens to be his number here that Crawford wants me to record for him. I know this is Alvin Piku. This is Piron in Bocage. Or Mama's Gone Goodbye. That's a great... That's a good tune. I do too. I think that's fine. So I'm going to cut this for the archives of music. Like I told you, my conception now isn't what it should be. But I'm sure that in a few weeks with a little practicing...
I'm sure with your experience and the natural talent and the way you played, it wouldn't be hard to come back. That's right.
How long, Don, do you think it will take you for you to get your lip back in shape?
Well, in the last three days I noticed quite a big improvement. And I think that within the next three weeks I will be able to cut at least four or five sides for the archives of music.
What kind of a horn do you use now?

Right now I'm using the King. The horn that was stolen from me, as I told you, a lot of my instruments have been stolen. I had a Selma that was stolen from me, incidentally with the mouthpiece that I played about 25 years. Which makes it more difficult now for me to get used to this mouthpiece that I'm trying. I've tried five or six of them.
Your Uncle Natty has a committee model Martin now, which she likes it. Quite a few people use those. Well, I've played Martin.
I've played Martin. I've found a Martin a good horn. But then, in playing heavy outdoor stuff I always have used a Holton or a C.G. Kahn.
A lot of the old timers over there used Kahn in the old days.
Oliver and I get Perez. You get a better reception on the outside.

Well, we don't want to bother you anymore, but unless there's something else you can think about, some of the other trumpet players you'd want to add about, anything about Manuel Perez or any of the others that you were especially close to?

Well, I used to like to meet up with Bunk Johnson when I... Oh, yeah. Bunk, yeah. I've recorded him. He's a particular friend of mine. I like Bunk. Well, Bunk got together in a Port Arthur one time. He said, I want to find that little fellow you all say, play so much trumpet. I want to see who he is. So, I happened to be sitting in a joint over there one night and in came Bunk Johnson. That's the first time I'd ever met him. And we had a session until five, six o'clock in the morning. And we turned to be great friends and every time I went to New Iberia where I paid Bunk a visit. And of course, I played with Orrin Page, which was called Lips Page. Yeah. He was with the Blue Devils. Yeah.
That was... Were you on that record?

No, I never cut with them. That was Count Basie was in there and I remember the band real well because I was with Troy's band and we had competition there. So, I would stay in my backyard as they say unless I was really needed.

They only cut that one record under that name. That's all. Walter Page and these Blue Devils. Blue Devils. That's correct. Yeah. I had that record at one time, Bill, and it ended up in Baker's collection.
Yeah. I had picked up one and it was Cracked one time. Everybody got a good one.

I had a good one. Like I said, Chester Clark was a very fine trumpet player, sweet trumpet player. Then there's another fellow I recall in New Orleans that I used to admire his playing and I think that a lot of the other fellows really did and all Mottwai. Oh yes.
We talked to his widow and his daughter still there. I never got to hear him.

I don't ever hear anyone. That's why I say a lot of these guys that give this information on jazz musicians of long ago, they seem to have contacted on various occasions some guy that really didn't know who these people were. Because if he did, he failed to recognize him.
And not very many people have mentioned him in the books or articles.

That's right. The same way with Mr. Morad. Now there's a few others. There was a great alto player in Dallas, Texas that played on the same style then that Johnny Hodges plays today. His name is Fred Murphy. Fred Murphy. That's right. Now nobody, they failed to mention him. Then you had Buster Bailey and guys like that in those days. They failed to mention. And all those guys were great, great musicians.
Well is Buster from around here?
Buster Bailey originally I think is from Dallas.
Well I know Buster quite well.

Now there is two Buster Bailey's. The one you're referring to I think is the one that was with Fletcher Henderson. Yeah. Well there is another one that was from Dallas that went to Europe and never came back. Well I don't know. Did he play Clarence also? Yes he was terrific. Really?
I didn't know that. Two of them.
Well I'll be right. Things we don't know.
I'll make a note of that.
That is also a course of course.

Buster Smith is still going on. He's been a great musician. But I understand Buster's lost a lot of his teeth and he's not doing much playing anymore. That's one thing in my favor, I have all of them.
Oh good, yeah. Your uncle Natty got false teeth both sets now.
Well is he playing?
He plays alright. He hasn't played much recently. He got those teeth before I left Chicago around 1955. He's had those false teeth now for six years. And he took it very slow but he can

play alright. Well Bunk Johnson had played. The only thing that was bad in Bunk's favor that was detrimental to him I'll say, he just couldn't stay off the bottle. The little fame that reached him at a late date as it was, I believe this, that if Bunk had taken it in strides that he would still be playing today.
Maybe he just had that heart attack, not heart attack, it was a stroke.
It was a stroke. I saw him. I brought Lloyd Armstrong to see him just a few days before he passed.
I just saw him a few days before too. That's what I saw. Oh excuse me. It's been real nice, you bet. I'll see you sometime. I get through here a couple times a year. Oh okay.
I'll see you goodnight.

I saw Bunk this Sunday before he died. No, he died on the... In the Iberia? Yeah, in the Iberia, whatever. The same, he died on July 7th. I saw him about four or five days before. So he must have been at that same week. Yeah. And I've been there at Mardi Gras all that same year.

Then too, I mean, just the short time that you have tonight, why there are so many other musicians that I would like to recognize that I know have been exceptionally good artists. Today, the trend that you have today, the musicians don't play music. They play noise.
Yeah, some of that rock and roll as well as the pop, I think too.

That's right. Even this running over the horn, the bebop or whatever they call it, there's no feeling there. And the first thing that I learned when I studied music was that music was the combination of sounds that was pleasing to the ear. Now when it deviates from there,
well you don't have anything. That's right. May I ask a question here? Do you know anything about Leroy's Dallas band Leroy who? Leroy's Dallas band. They recorded on Columbia, Bill.

I think that was a part of the Blue Moon Chasers. Now I'm not sure. Well, who were the Blue Moon Chasers? It was a group of young fellows that had gotten together in Bud Johnson. That's a tenor player. You might know him. Bud Johnson was one of the original members.
He's still playing in the management. That's right. Well, that was the Blue Moon Chasers.
That was in the days of Troy Floyd. Yeah. 26, 27 and 28. That's right. Then of course you had another great trumpet player in the Southwest.
How about Tommy Howell? Did you know Tommy Howell? No, I didn't. Did you ever hear of a trombone player by the name of Sonny Clapp?
I knew Sonny Clapp.
You did?
That was a white trombone player. Yeah. That's right. Yeah. Yeah, Sonny Clapper. I used to laugh at his name.
That's how I remember him. Yeah. Well now, Tommy Howell played with Sonny Clapp. He played a little like Biderback.
That's right. No, Biderback's a trumpet player. Now the other fellow, the other trumpet player I'm referring to in the Southwest that was T Holder. What? T Holder.
Who did he play?
He had the original Clouds of Joy that Kirk took over. That was his band. T Holder's club.
How do you spell his name? T. T. Yeah.
His name is Torrance, but they said T. T. H-O-L-D-E-R. Holder. That's right.
He was a good trumpet player.
Beautiful.
Beautiful sounds.
Kurt, Clouds of Joy. That's right.
That was a good band. Oh, man, I should say.
Well, I don't want to keep you any longer as I say. I know you have to get up and work in the morning. You have to get up and work in the morning so I think we'd better close.
If you think that you've had sufficient talk.
Yes, I think we covered your life pretty well. There's nothing else about the real old days when you first started that you can think of that you've come back to mind.
Well, like I said, there's so much that it would take so long.

Yeah, actually to get it all organized. We could go on and on and on and I could get it. But I think it covers in a general way your life pretty well from the very first days and I'm glad to get a little information about your father too.
Yes, well.
Because I'm afraid we won't get to talk to him. He couldn't be available to talk much longer. I mean since he seems to be going blind and all.

That's right. Well, there's only one thing about his blindness. His sight could be saved if he would only go get an operation. You think it would? Sure, I had a doctor here guarantee the operation but right now he's reluctant to have it. But he was just about ready to have it two months ago. I don't know what changed his mind.
That age though, pretty good age, 82. Yeah, but the doctor said that he had a lot of strength.
I had, my aunt had her eyes operated on when she was 17.
